**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks, a silent metronome counting down the seconds until I must begin. A thousand words—how heavy they feel when the mind is a storm of half-formed thoughts. I could write about the rain tapping against my window, each drop a tiny percussionist in an orchestra of gray. Or perhaps I could unravel the memory of my grandmother’s hands, how they kneaded dough with the same patience she used to braid my hair when I was small.

But no, the words resist. They coil like smoke, slipping through my fingers before I can grasp them. Writing is an act of faith—faith that the right words will come, that the page will hold them gently, that someone, somewhere, will read them and feel less alone.

I think of the first time I understood the power of words. I was eight, curled under a blanket with a flashlight, devouring a book about a girl who could fly. The words lifted me, too, not in body but in spirit. For the first time, I realized that stories were bridges—between worlds, between hearts, between the self you are and the self you might become.

Now, as an adult, I chase that feeling. I write to remember, to forget, to make sense of the chaos. Some days, the words flow like a river; other days, they drip like a leaky faucet. Today, they are stubborn. They hide in the shadows of my mind, whispering, *You don’t have enough. You never do.*

But I write anyway.

Because a thousand words are not just a count—they are a landscape. A thousand words can be a love letter, a manifesto, a eulogy. They can be the shape of a life, the echo of a laugh, the silence after a scream. They can be the difference between being seen and being invisible.

I wonder if the words I choose will matter. Will they linger like the scent of rain on hot pavement, or fade like footprints in the sand? The fear of insignificance is a shadow that follows every writer. Yet, we write. We must.

Perhaps these words are not for anyone else. Maybe they are just for me—a way to untangle the knots in my chest, to name the things that ache. Writing is how I make sense of the world, how I stitch together the fragments of my days into something resembling meaning.

The cursor still blinks. The page is no longer blank, but it is not yet full. I have used some of my thousand words, and still, there is more to say. There is always more to say.

So I keep writing. Because words, even imperfect ones, are how we reach for each other in the dark.
